text:
sam: Hey—seeing an intermittent client-side hang when cancelling streaming requests under high QPS (50-100 rps). It only shows up on the Go SDK (http2) and seems tied to sustained backpressure + batching. Repro below, anyone seen this?

maria: Hmm, vaguely. Prod had something similar — streams would hang and connections would pile up, but we blamed a proxy first.

kevin: Can you paste a minimal repro or the transport config?

sam: Sure — simplified snippet from the client:

sam: ```go
tr := &http.Transport{
    MaxIdleConns: 200,
    MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 200,
    IdleConnTimeout: 90 * time.Second,
    DisableKeepAlives: false,
    TLSHandshakeTimeout: 10 * time.Second,
}
client := &http.Client{Transport: tr}

ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
defer cancel()
req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "POST", url, bytes.NewReader(payload))
req.Header.Set("Connection", "keep-alive")
resp, err := client.Do(req)
if err != nil { return err }
// streaming read
reader := bufio.NewReader(resp.Body)
for {
    line, err := reader.ReadBytes('\n')
    if err != nil { break }
    // process...
}
// missing explicit drain/close in some code paths
```

sam: When cancel(ctx) is called during burst, goroutines leak and we eventually hit connection starvation. Logs show many goroutines stuck in http2.(*clientConnReadLoop).readFrame or in net/http2.readFrameHeader.

maria: Two quick things to check: 1) Are you always `defer resp.Body.Close()`? 2) Do you `io.Copy(ioutil.Discard, resp.Body)` before close when aborting mid-stream? If you don't drain, http2 may hold the stream open.

kevin: Also try toggling `MaxIdleConnsPerHost` down or up — we've seen weird scheduling with very high values on 1.20 runtime. Another knob: `Transport.ResponseHeaderTimeout` so the client won't wait forever on a stalled stream.

jen: My note: Go's http2 transport needs explicit connection reuse safety — if you cancel a request you should close body and maybe call `req.Close = true` for the non-reuse case. But `req.Close` is deprecated for HTTP/2 effects, so prefer draining + Close.

sam: Good call — currently some fast-fail paths call cancel but don't drain. I'll add a small wrapper that ensures `resp.Body.Close()` and drains in a goroutine on cancel.

maria: Also check if you have middlebox NGHTTP2 settings or a proxy that buffers for a bit and then RST_STREAMs. If the server RSTs while client is trying to cancel, http2 internals can get weird.

kevin: If you can reproduce locally, try a tiny binary that runs 100 goroutines making streaming calls and cancels half after random delays. That helped us isolate the race earlier.

sam: I attached a stress harness to the thread gist: https://gist.github.com/redwood/stress-h2-repro (pseudo link). Repro shows leak in ~30s at 80rps.

infra-bot: CI: integration-tests/stress-h2 started on staging (build #4521) :hourglass_flowing_sand:

jen: One more idea — set Transport.DisableCompression = true in case compression interacts with streaming chunking under backpressure.

maria: And if you suspect a Go runtime bug, try with Go 1.21 vs 1.22 (we had improvements around http2 idle timeouts).

sam: Ok will run matrix: {Go: [1.20,1.21,1.22], MaxIdleConnsPerHost: [50,200], IdleConnTimeout: [30s,90s], DisableCompression: [true,false]} and report. I'll also add a small helper that always drains on cancel.

kevin: If you get consistent repro on 1.22 file a small issue with a self-contained program — go stdlib folks are good at repros.

sam: Will do. Also going to add an integration test to our client repo and tag eng-infra for infra limits.

jen: Ping me or @maria on the PR and I'll review the transport/routing changes.

sam: Thanks all — appreciate the quick tips. I'll update thread with results. :thumbsup:
